extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator; readers interested in poetry, theatre, dance, and polite manners (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and observations on what makes sublime epic poetry (Milton's Battle of Angels), effective theatrical performance, and the art/usefulness of dancing; includes evaluative points and examples. Focuses on qualities authors and performers should cultivate and what readers/audiences should expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's imagination should 'rise above himself' in great scenes (e.g., Milton in describing the Battle of Angels), producing images of grandeur and terror appropriate to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold, elevated imagery to match a sublime subject; example quotations: 'The Authors Imagination was so inflam'd with this great Scene of Action, that wherever he speaks of it, he rises, if possible, above himself.' Avoid underwhelming or petty images in such scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Mean or Trivial Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain exactness of judgment to 'avoid every thing that might appear light or trivial' when describing great or terrible subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of puerilities and wantonness that turn sublime passages into burlesque; example anti-patterns cited include Claudian's extravagant islands and rivers which verge on ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Use of Classical Precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ hints and devices from ancient poets (Homer, Virgil, Claudian) but improve upon them and omit their puerilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate the grandeur and effective particulars of the ancients (e.g., Homer's mounting of battles) while avoiding literal copying of their absurdities; Milton 'has taken every thing that is sublime in these several Passages, and composes out of them' better images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and Foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Great scenes should be prepared for by earlier passages that raise readers' expectation and qualify the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior hints and buildup so the reader is ready for a grand scene; Addison notes Milton 'having raised his Readers Expectation, and prepared him for it by several Passages in the preceding Books.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation and Varied Strokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative or poetic combats should rise and improve, with successive strokes increasing in horror and grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure battles so engagements build one above another (Homeric model); ensure variety of sublime images across the sequence to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime Yet Natural Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most extraordinary images should appear natural and agreeable to the reader's notion of the subject (e.g., a battle of angels should employ images fitting divine combat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose images (shouts, thunder, flying darts, torn-up mountains) that, though grand, cohere with the implied world of the poem; avoid incongruous or absurd combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious Boldness (Plausible Invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold or novel conceits (such as giving artillery to rebel angels) are acceptable when they plausibly suit the character and aims of the agents involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A daring thought that fits the agents' motives and the poem's logic is praiseworthy; provide reasoning so the reader accepts the invention ('as such a pernicious Invention may be well supposed to have proceeded from such Authors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sacred and Classical Allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate poetical passages from Scripture and classical epics to enrich imagery and authority (e.g., Ezekiel for the Messiah's chariot, Psalms for the Messiah's commission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions should strengthen the scene and feel congruent with the poem's milieu; cite models that amplify the intended grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Burlesque; Maintain Gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep images from slipping into ludicrousness—excessive wildness (e.g., tossing whole islands) tends toward burlesque rather than sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance wild imagination with restraint and plausibility; prefer lifted, suggestive imagery over grotesque extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Pacing and Relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermix speeches, reflections, similitudes, and other 'resting-places' to give readers opportunities to recover amid sustained sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contrasts and moments of relief so attention can be recharged; Addison praises Milton for interspersing diversions 'that he might come fresh to his great Action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Familiar Particulars vs. Universal Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Select particulars (like named mountains in Homer) when they augment imagery; when unavailable, compose equivalent majestic images without lapsing into triviality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named, well-known particulars can intensify an image, but a poet may compensate through compositional skill when such particulars aren't available (Milton's plucking up 'seated Hills' is given as a successful substitute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured Restraint (Controlled Power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a mighty figure (e.g., the Messiah) should be described as holding back force when appropriate—restraint can heighten majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that show a superior being 'put[ting] not forth half his Strength' demonstrate moral intent and grandeur; avoid portraying omnipotence as indiscriminate destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Natural Terrible Phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ elements like thunder, lightning, earthquakes, and the rattling of chariots to lift the reader's imagination in great combats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These effects should be integrated artfully to augment the scene's terror and sublimity rather than as mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness of Judgment in Blending Learning and Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine learned allusions and strong invention with prudence so that erudition supports the imagination without overwhelming or cluttering it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning should be a help not a show-off; Addison credits Milton with 'all the Helps he could meet with among the Ancient Poets' yet united with his own genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing as an Art of Deportment
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing cultivates 'a becoming Motion, Gesture and Aspect' and improves one's mien; small accomplishments like dancing materially affect social grace and presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and practice harmony and composure of limbs; dancing should be part of education because habitual carriage improves general behaviour and performance (example: Booth's majesty in a step could be enhanced by dancing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing Should Be Systematized and Taught
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of dancing ought to have fundamental rules, an historical account, and instruction to correct 'gross and growing Errors' and to improve both performers and spectators' judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate treatises and masters who set down parts, uses, and standards; spectators informed by rules are better judges and dancers better performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and Usefulness of Dancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing is both an accomplishment and beneficial exercise: it refines behaviour, aids social display, and may be allied to higher arts if systematized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter the view of dancing as a mere trifle or mechanical capering; argue for its antiquity, utility, and potential for development into a regular science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and Composure of Motion
rubrics_metrics.description: True dancing demonstrates harmony and composure in limbs and countenance—'the true Harmony and Composure of his Limbs and Countenance' distinguishes good dancers and graceful persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should look for ease, proportion, and reasoned motion rather than only natural features; habit and instruction convert natural mien into polished grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of Language in Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers in tragedy should be intelligible—audiences expect to understand the meaning of sentences and not to be obscured by unnecessary obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly abstruse diction or delivery that confuses; Addison records Sir Roger's delight that 'there is not a single Sentence in this Play that I do not know the Meaning of.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical Expression and Movement in Acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Majestick and great conceptions are expressed through motion (e.g., an actor's step or march can convey elevation and character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should cultivate deportment and movement (dancing can help); Booth's march to his throne is cited as an instance where physical carriage communicates high conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/Historical Awareness in Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should be informed by knowledge of ancient and modern practices—understanding antiquity (e.g., Greek/Roman dances, Homeric battles) aids evaluation and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the historical forms and uses of an art to judge its modern state and to propose constructive reforms (as in the proposed 'History of Dancing').
